newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia admits some opposition election victories.
newsitem.headline: Serbia admits some opposition election victories.

text.p: Embattled by six straight weeks of street protests, the Serbian government admitted on Friday that opposition parties had won some municipal elections later annulled by the ruling Socialists (SPS).

But its response to OSCE investigators who confirmed SPS misconduct made no mention of the elections' biggest prize, the Belgrade city assembly, and said results in several key cities including Serbia's second largest, Nis, remained unclear.

Serbia's pro-democracy movement, the Zajedno (Together) coalition, rejected the government reply as a pack of lies and vowed to soldier on with demonstrations until its victories were reinstated in all disputed districts.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, strongman of federal Yugoslavia, has remained silent on a report by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on the disputed municipal elections drawn up last week by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez after a fact-finding mission.
The SPS-run mainstream media have denounced Zajedno demonstrators as alleged stooges of a bullying West.

Western governments have warned Milosevic to recognise the election outcome in full and democratise Serbia or be denied financial aid for the economy, in ruins from SPS corruption and 54 months of U.N. sanctions lifted a year ago.

In a letter from Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic to the OSCE, the government conceded Zajedno won the majority in nine wards of Belgrade. But he said nothing about the Yugoslav capital's policy-making city assembly and maintained the outcome in Nis, the original hotbed of protests, remained uncertain.
"When competent authorities establish the facts, the results of the elections (in Nis) will be known," Milutinovic said.

He acknowledged Zajedno won the cities of Uzice, Kragujevac and Zrenjanin but said no party garnered a majority in Pirot, Pancevo and Jagodina. Milutinovic called for more data on six other municipalities in question.
The OSCE-commissioned report said unequivocally that Zajedno had won the vote in all municipalities invalidated by the SPS.
The organisation's decision-making permanent council planned a special session later on Friday to study Gonzalez's report and Milutinovic's answer, officials of the security forum said.
Milutinovic said Gonzalez's call that the will of the people be respected was precisely his government's position.
"However, it is obvious that all this should be established within the legal institutions, on the basis of law and regulations of the Republic of Serbia," he said.
Milutinovic stressed Belgrade agreed with Gonzalez that the crisis had to be solved "through implementation of adequate procedures and in a spirit of dialogue and cooperation".
Zajedno leaders vowed to continue rallies despite government concessions and tens of thousands of whistle-blowing protesters massed in Belgrade on Friday for the 47th consecutive day.

Vuk Draskovic, leader of the Serbian Renewal Movement which together with the Democratic Party and Civil Alliance comprises Zajedno, described Milutinovic's letter as a smokescreen that effectively spurned OSCE recommendations.

"This is the typical way of Milosevic -- lies, tricks to (outwit) the international community...We reject this shameful letter of Milutinovic, a letter of lies and manipulations," Draskovic told Reuters.

Zoran Djindjic, another Zajedno leader, dismissed fears of the daily street rallies boiling over into civil war, saying Milosevic's authority had declined so much there was little danger of major violence.
However a 10-day-old Interior Ministry ban on street marches has heightened the risk of confrontations with police.

"The basis of Milosevic's authority has been diminished to such an extent that he cannot provoke a civil war because there are not enough people who would want, or have an interest to, wage war for him," Djindjic said.
"The only conceivable form of violence is conflict between demonstrators and police, but it cannot be of large proportion. The danger is not as major as (previously) supposed."

Dissension over the annulment of the elections has surfaced in the army, the Serbian Orthodox Church and even the security police, all mainstays of autocratic leftist government in federal Yugoslavia up to now.

Analysts said debate was raging in Milosevic's circle between moderates prepared to risk slackening the SPS grip on power to open the Western financial pipeline and hardliners ready to hunker down behind a siege economy.
